title: Percy Humphrey Band: Percy Humphrey, Jim Robinson, Ernest Roubleau, Josiah Frazier Interview, 1972-02-29

blocks.x: I'm away from his wife until he gets to be 21 years old. I said, well, then, 21 years old. They're married, but he can't be with his wife until he gets 21 years old. Why that's something that you know couldn't work? All right. We're playing, we're playing the music. They're jumping in the sand right close to the river. And the will is up there. They're having a good time.

. . . . . . . It was 21, street they called Corner and Roman. It was like you said, two, that time they had wagons. It was Punch with his band and Kid Rene with his band, but he happened to have two corners. Rick, I was playing with him that Sunday. And the first number they played, I was just, I think it was Panama. And then they came back and Punch picked up a good blues number. No, I don't think nobody in the world them days could beat Punch playing a blues number. Couldn't beat that man with a blues number. Couldn't beat him. Couldn't beat him. So Rene came back with a number they called Don Honk-a-Tonk Town. You see, that's from the district days. Well, that's the district that was still running at that time. But they told me the right title was Give Me Your Money, You're Drunk. Yeah. Yeah. That's the right name for it. That's the right title for it, yeah. So Rene and them came back with that number. He played some men. See, them days, a cornette player, you could be the greatest trombone or cloud of drum in the world. They featured the cornettes. That's where they get the name Kid. Rene blew some many chords against one man. Then Rick, I blew some many chords, you see. And when they got through with that, like you said, people trot up their hats and caps in the street. They want them trucks to go, you understand? That was on a Sunday evening. And from that day on, I took a light to that number. I'm honky-tonk town. I don't know if it had words or not to it, whether it was orchestration, I don't know.
I know where it comes from, but I never know it being orchestrated. But the boys got the number. The boys got the number. The boys got the number. You want to bring out. I know that.

All I can tell you during the district, when we young men like that go around there, the police will take a strap. When I'm 68 years old at present, and I just called almost the last part of the district. I wouldn't tell you a lie that I played in the district, but I know about it. And we go around there, they just take, with being boys, they take this strap and they beat you on your backside and chase you out. They know what you do is just scare you. And we respect men to them days, you understand? It's not any going person. Yeah. In case you'll just run us away from around there. Yeah, you have to be a man to go over there. Yeah.

When I went over there, ooh, I just went over to the base and looked at all them pretty people past. I said, Jesus Christ, I want to be 21 years old. But I didn't call it. You know what I mean? Mary said, oh, the Lord said, oh, he's a man now. Yeah, he's a boy. Oh, Jesus Christ. I said, I want to go by his daddy and lose some to all the first jobs and playing. I was a young fellow there too, you know. But otherwise, you know, I never let no girls then know. I was busy with music. I didn't like them. And then girls that come to my house and my sister lost saved with Jim. I said, oh, I'm not a girl. I said, I don't put no girls. That's right. I had one girl. He said, her name was quite true. And I love that girl, understand? But I would never tell them about the mothers. They would be flashing. I said, oh, Lord. I like one.

I like one. You see, in my time, I know Jim as old as I am, when we go to the balls, you remember we were talking to the great economy hall. And they like that number stumbling. I'm going to bring you to around 21 and 22. Them numbers come out. We go to them big balls, like the church, you heard the Jim was giving the festival. Sam up there playing the music. I don't know if you're stuck about that. I'm up there watching Alfred on the drum and looking at the band play that number. You understand? And the rest of the day, you're stuck about no dancing. And you couldn't move me from that bandstand. Why did they call it economy hall, though? Oh, that's a French name, isn't it? French name, yeah. That's a French name, yeah. That was a cheap. It wasn't cheap, economy.
No, that's big society.
No, that's big organizations. Oh, society, benovine organizations. It's like the Jean's Army. Oh, let's go Creole. Part of French Creole. Then we had, oh, we had lots of benovine organizations.

We used to be playing with people having a good time dancing. Sure, man. We used to have so much dance here in this town until we didn't know who to go and play for. We had so many engagements. We were wondering who to play for.

Then the people used to use the funeral bands, the brass band, what the better they did. Prosperity, perseverance, it's all different organizations. All societies. All societies, yeah. What no insurance system was it? No, no, no, no. What no insurance system was it?
No insurance system.
No insurance system. No insurance system. No, we had insurance but not.
What nicks?
Not the.
Publicers like it's done. The society is a barrier.
How they do, y'all pay so much, maybe some organization 75 cents a month to do.
And give you a good funeral to them.

Yeah, when you lose your members, your dead members, you'll be taxed. Some of them 50 cents. Now my daddy belongs to the Prosperity. Used to be that, you remember the old, Hall and Vera, Brother Hall's Church there. The old Vera between Boeben and St. Anthony. Preservative? That's where that would be Brother Hall's Church. The Prosperity Society used to meet there. And that's the name that used to be the way prior to that. And I belong to young men back in New Jersey. That's the way around the night ward. They bury it with them. We lose them, remember? Oh, yeah. They was fine 50 cents. That's for the music fees. That's right. To the brass band.

Look at the fuel cost here now. Four and five, $6,000. You got a bear person in, save what? $50 in. Big fuel, isn't it? Look at the cost here now. That's true. You got to go in the thousand now. This is the bear person now. Oh, yeah.
So could King Oliver play then? King Oliver?

Yeah. Oh, man. What's he? If his name was King, what's nobody about that man, man? Who got food that man? If he was King, what's nobody about that man, man? No, no. If you're king and you prove that you're king, I'm going to jump on you? No, no. Let you know. That's what I'm going to have. Oh, yeah. Well, I thought maybe you were older than him.
You could remember that. Who?

No, no. King Oliver was a man listening, playing music, long listening. Came up and playing music, long. See, I just listened. I taught in tramo in 1970. Them people had been playing. And Poetsy? That's right. People had been playing, man. And I learned fast. Because I stole what I got. I stole that. Everything I learned in tramo, I stole it. I go by you, Dick, how you make that dick? I take that and go and, I'm not spiraling, but I'm going to make it, and I get it together. New York, but I'm going to put more than you put, and you let me. Put more to it.

You were talking about the number of jobs you had, and how there was a dance, you know, every night, more than one place. And it sounds as though New Orleans was, you know, really living for music in those days. This is the way it sounded to us, say, New York. Every time we said jazz, of course, all we thought of was New Orleans.

It sounded like the whole town was nothing but one big, constant jazz band. What was it like? Well, in a way, I could say it my way about it. You didn't have no radios. I mean, television and all that. Jukebox and most of them. And any little house party will use. Maybe ordinary people will get a drum and a piano, sometimes a clarinet or a corner, a three-piece band, and give house parties. Plus, some people give lawn parties to have a regular six, seven-piece band. Give lawn parties. Like, they didn't open yard during the summer nights. Then we had Millenburg out there. We had West End. We had Bucktown. Had camps out there on the old lake. You need a Monday to go by, some band would be playing out at them camps. You understand? I mean, you call it picnits. Is that, now, you said Millenburg. Yeah, that's the leg function train. We used to call it Millenburg. Millenburg, yeah, Millenburg. Okay.
What kind of a place was that?
It was a summer swimming place. Some people had their houses, camped, built right over the water. The water. Had like these trusses. Still got a chance. Some parts of the sea. Haunt your dream?
Yes.
Still got the camps. No, going out the little woods like this, still got a few camps.
But the camps yet?
Like back to the section.

And beautiful camps too. And the band used to beat Buck one another. Oh yeah. Just like, I'm playing for you over here, my band, another band over there, we're walking in the next one, he playing trumpet, we're going to beat Buck one another and stand to the next one. Oh man, what fun man. Yeah. Boy, it's not no fun that could just be years ago. The junctures ain't got sense enough to take, to finish what we come through. That's true.
Tell them about the bankers, we call them bunkers them days.

The music we're playing now in these places, like on the street and everything, it's hardly much pleasure for the musicians or the people that are being entertained because it's constant. Of course they have to do it in modern times, you know what I mean, to turn it over and entertain the tourists and whatnot. During the time these gentlemen were talking about that, we'd be out there and play about in the whole hour. We didn't play no more than about five or six tunes. Is that right, Ruth? Right. Right. And the people would have time to sit down and relax and enjoy themselves, whatever refreshment they had for sale or whatever they brought with them. It was just like a regular country gathering, you know what I mean, even though you were in the city or in the city limits, see. But now everybody's fighting. The musicians don't understand. They're busting their jaws and everything to try to keep everybody happy. The people sitting out there, they, I don't want to see how they can sit in there sometimes. It's so loud. There's no music or nothing. They just go a lot of blasting and whatnot. Yeah. See, but that's the way life is now. But at that time, everybody enjoyed the music, the people that's making the music, and the people that they were making the music for. It was just one big gathering and everybody having plenty of fun. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. See? So I don't know. Imagine in some places in this world there's people still living that way. I don't know. But all the pleasure has been driven out of it now. Oh, we sit up there and we enjoy it because we play from our arts. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. It's a whole lot of treasure to it now. At that time, it was a pleasure. Yeah, because the hours was long. You'd take the hours long. Oh, you'd play from 8 o'clock or 7 o'clock to 3 or 4 o'clock in the morning. Yeah, that's right.
I ain't going to do nothing.
I mean, and those people would think. I ain't going to do it.
No, no.

People would still be there every time. No, I ain't going to do it. Sure. And you talk about nothing, boy. People used to walk from camp to camp. Sure. Right. You want to be promenading all night. All night and night.

Your friend got campers that you invite you and your wife or some of your friends. Sure. Come to our camp, our band. Now you walk in, just all night, camp and stuff. And them trump and stuff, and Tramon talk like that. Pa, pa, pa, pa, pa, man. You can just give them.
Take the labor there now.
We don't celebrate that. Tramon's talking about, I'm telling you.

Years ago, all the long showmans, the skillmans. Yeah, that's right. They used to form different brass bands. And they'd all start, and they'd meet at a street they called Elk's Place. You see, that's right on right now. They call that Basin Street, I mean, and the Simon Boulevard. Well, all the bands from different parts of the city, they'd all meet there. Now, them people would have their parades all day long. Then at night, they'd have a brass band and a regular six or seven piece jazz band to play. And that goes, like you say, four, five o'clock in the morning at the fairground, the old fairground, where they have the races at, and this booth's there all night long. You understand?

About 10 o'clock in the day. About 10 o'clock in the day, eh? Until all night. Sure, man. You look like you done had your fun, you done, what you been doing, then you go home, go dressing, and took a bath, and say, I'm going to the fairground and have me some water.

Well, I'll say this much, since I've been fooling with any kind of music, the Vixalayan jazz is the only music that you can really understand and give your most spirit to dance and everything else that I haven't seen myself. Well, that's what you do. Of course, I'm not down in the ground. You call it when you play. When you play, you see. Like that. You got a bad melody. But ever since I've been a man, and before I know how to play any kind of music, I heard Vixalayan brass band play and everything else. And I said to myself, that's a wonderful music that they were playing. I said that to myself. They didn't know anything about it.

And long ago, long ago, you know what I was playing? People want to play now what they can sing, what they understand. Would you play a melody? You ain't no way. You see, you take a- And then? That's right. That's right. That melody, if you don't listen, I don't want to dispute the band where they're playing now, them rock and roll band. I can play a tough too, but I want some melody where I can follow. I want to play a melody. Let you understand you, your family. Jim Robinson playing a melody on a trombone. I want to sing it to you. What I'm making there?
You know where you're humming that? I had a dream.
You play as that.

So far as the rock and roll. I keep instrument to play rock and roll in case if somebody jumped me up. I keep that kind of instrument to play rock and roll. But see like this, this ain't no rock and roll instrument.

You see, let me tell them this too. You see they speak about saying music is a universal language. My first time going overseas in 1966. We had a place they called Copenhagen, Munich, Germany. Because it was working out of Frankfurt, Germany. The first night we played, the first number you played, everybody sounds looking at you in Germany. You think they're not. They're taking that music. They couldn't understand our language. And I'm from the south down here. My way of speaking, where the kicks will come out when we get into these different restaurants and girls we serve. They don't understand my language. They don't understand them. But some of the places have an interpreter. But that bandstand, when we played, see how they played that first set, the house came down. Screaming and clapping. You see how that music can reach them? Now where the kicks come out, like I had them laughing by the Pop Foster. Now I've been different parts of Germany. I worked Dusseldorf. I worked Frankfurt. I worked Baden-Baden. I worked Berlin. I stood up there with the All-Star Band 66. Then I went back there in 67 with George Lewis and them group. And we didn't play Berlin. Then we played London, England in 66. But like I said, but in Germany, England people understood us good. And when I went to Copenhagen, the place they called, in Switzerland, they understand us. And then Sweden the same way. But in Germany, that's why we run into trouble with our language. But that music can reach them people. You see? Yeah, they understand that, man. Music reach them all over the world. In the world, yeah. That lingo is something.
Especially the Dixieland jazz. It reaches so many, many people. What about keeping time? Did y'all keep good time there? Did people dance to the bands?

That's what I made in the dance bar, didn't you? When you hit the ball. There ain't no big band. There ain't no big band. There ain't no big band. There ain't no big band. The band didn't play as fast as they're playing. They people called that circus music. But if you were the colored balls, all the white dancers, that's all you had was jazz bands. Now you had good bands now in them times. The band he played was a lot of games of my life. And Sam Morgan Band, in the section where I live at, if you get Sam Morgan Band, you're going to draw the people. I'm taking it from 1920, 1921, all like that, bringing up to 29 and 30. You see, if you wouldn't get Sam Morgan Band in that Creole section, then people are going to come to your dance. Now they used Economy Hall. You see? They used the Jean's Amie. Or they used the... Friends Amie. The France Amie. Then you used the... The Jean's Amie, they're on Robinson Street, too. Yeah, you got the France Amie. That's on Robinson, between St. Anthony and Boydman. But that gang. Now another band they liked was Kid René Band. Economy Hall and all that gang. You see, you take... Carburetos. Yeah, Carburetos. The Vegetable Packers. All them people used to work on the Cater Street for Chris Roode, packing vegetables in these big barrels that you call sugar barrels. They ship it to the north. You call it the... That people used to get periods, too, once a year. Just like the Jolly Boys and so forth like that. That people get what they call it. Vegetable Packers. Yeah. They give big dancers. Oh, man. That's all the music they had.
That's a... They had some dancers from their heart.
Yeah. Oh, shouters, waltzes.
They do you good like they eat their sands to see the people dance. That's right.
Hoss, can you play a shouters? You gotta try it. You understand? I don't know if you can beat it all right now, but we gotta get together. We gotta try a shouters. It's about a 4-4-10. Yeah.
Somebody threw out a line about two minutes ago, and then it went by. You said the phrase circus music.

Oh, yeah. I said that. That means like some of these black people. Well, I'll tell you that. Since I've been making these tours with the Preservation Hall band, we had the young people talk. We didn't like jazz because we thought it was too brassy. It was like... You know, like sometimes you're making a commercial. Like a fast commercial, you understand, it's too brassy. I said, well, no, baby, you got the thing wrong. I said, this music we playing now, people used to dance by this music. And we didn't play it too fast. Something called one step, two step and slow drag. They used the term slow drag, you see. And like a blues, you know, and a nice foxtrot and all like that. But some of these bands really played and that made them cheering on the metal songs. All the tours I came to backstage, they tell us all that.

But I will still say so. I will still, this is my motto. I like the music. The way you play it the way you want to play it. But I love it, understand? Because I don't know the other way to do what I'm doing. Well, you come up with that. And I can't change it. I can't change it. But I don't say that rock and roll is good for people who like it. But I don't say that's... Them boys don't... And all them boys come from school. School band. Them boys can read. Don't you worry what they can't do. They think... We've got plenty of good rock and roll musicians. I met a gang of them. You understand? Something in two... No, that's what we met, you know... San Francisco. Graceful Deed. What?

Had that million dollar... Not a million dollar head. About $30,000 equipment. What? Graceful Deed. What? Who are them people stuck? Graceful Deed. San Francisco. Yeah. We talk with them people there. They said the amplifiers was right. Them boys. Fillmore West. And there was...

They went to a lot playing. This was down low. And you could, every man was doing this, you could enjoy it. Man can't do drummers. One of the things. Yeah. Two drummers. When we got there, I said look here. Boy.

How much of the old music came from, I think, we were talking to Dick yesterday afternoon, I was thinking that, you know, entrance of the gladiators, that one, it goes into That's A Plenty. Oh, yeah. Right? Well, it's close. It might have some positives. I wonder how much early jazz came out of martial music, brass band music, I mean music that never was written for the 2-4 beat, that was written for the 1-3 beat. I wonder how much early jazz came out of brass band music. You know, brass band music. At one time, from my understanding, at one time, that was practically all you had, brass band music, like the suits and marches and all that stuff. See, that's the reason you hear the phrase about circus music, see? Yeah. Circus will hit a town and to attract attention, they'd take any march. Yeah. We had so many honesty goodness rehearsals, you know, guys would hardly miss a note. Oh, yeah. They'd play it on, what's that, what you call that, that double time, see? Oh, yeah, yeah. They'd play it on that double time. Bop, bop, bop, bop, bop. Yeah. And everybody, they wouldn't miss a step or nothing else. They wouldn't miss a step or nothing else. That drum all he could do, the beat, they'd say boom, the snare drum, say bop, bop, bop. That's right. And they marched and they're just, you know what I mean? Oh, school children, man. I can't do that. Let's go. You think sometimes this military stuff was kind of fast, but those circuses, when they say circus music, that means you're racehorses, see? Yeah, they're going, man. They're going. But now, to get back to what you said, the whole lot of the music we play now, I'd say is derivative from a whole lot of marches is copied right behind them. The only thing is, well, your marches, your rhythm going to say, chink, chink, you see? And they don't go that way. And I said they double it up, see? That's the way they do it now. But like if you, the brass band stuff, that bass drum hit one that snap drum answer. Anson, yeah. See? Your bass horn say, whoop, the mellophones and whatnot, they make the answer. Yeah. See? But now, instead of one doing just one section on the, on the, on the, on the, what, the phrase or whatever you call it, they're doubling up all the way on it. See? They're single for a while. Yeah. See? But they give it the pep and the shove that, what we consider in jazz, see? They improvise on it, see? They add to it, to it, what, the original score, see? And they play it the way they feel it should be played. Forget about the music and the way the, the brass bands been playing it. See? That is that particular type brass band. Yeah, yeah. See? The military bands and the school bands and whatnot. Any of you give much to the theory that jazz came out of spirituals? Does this, you know, does this hold much more? Yeah.
Well, what do you mean, about special hymns? Yeah. The things we play come out, or the hymn books in the church which you sing.
But he mean, yeah.
Yeah, but, yeah. They come out of hymn books that you sing in church. It's written down, the fellas, write it down, give a man his part. That's what you, you understand? It was.

A certain portion of it, a certain feeling of it. That's right. That's right, I'm telling you. The expression did come from the people in slavery. They would make, make the, what we call the melody up. Yeah. Make the woods up and everything. And you could hear that all through the woods and everything. Humming good. And a whole lot of these musicians and whatnot, these composers, at that time, they copied from those people. Right. See? By them knowing how to build up with the music, they could set it to music. That's where it originated. Oh, right. That feeling. The feeling of the spirituals and whatnot. A person. That's where it was.

The closest to work with the, it's never been written. It didn't came from New York no way. That's a special book. Well, that's a funeral, though. It's just a funeral. It's not, it's not, it's not. It's a funeral. It's just a funeral. It's a funeral.
It's just a funeral. It's just a funeral. It's just a funeral.

It's just a funeral. It's just a funeral. It's just a funeral. It's just a funeral. Because if it had been written, listened from New York music, probably wouldn't have it. But that came out of the book, with the church with you. The book to you. You'd go somewhere and sing. You'd get your book to you. Just to close with you.

Jim, I may be wrong, but I thought his reference was, even before the tour, the way that people used to sing it and moan and groan, even before the book was printed. That was my idea. That's what I thought. I thought that was your question. I didn't even know that. You answered it right.
Just reference an answer, though, because... You see, I bring that letter to the end. That music, you both answered my question.
You would have that, too.

That music, you would have that, too. You would have that, because... You're like, you had a phrase out once that... You'd go on it easy. That much. Wait a while, Jim. Let me tell you about the place they call, right up here in Mississippi, where it got that big shipyard. It's called Singing Rimbled, Pasigula. They claim, what he used the term, singing river, is they're doing the slaves. The lots of slaves come in the side, drown themselves. Nowadays, I don't know if that's true or not. They claim they all walked into that river and drowned themselves, just humming. And the phrase came out in the later years that you could still hear them voices humming like that. You understand? It's called Singing River. Pasigula, Mississippi. That's right. Yeah, but Poison gave you the right definition about it. That's just taking fun during the slavery time. That's right. People and master people can read and have better training. They just could cover that off. And that... Well, I actually seen people in my career playing music, actually sitting down there, just like a big Poison do shorthand writing. It's sketching the band off. I seen that done when he said we've been tourists. See, I noticed this thing. I'm playing the drum. Yeah. When you've been a player, I'd be watching that audience out there.

See, this is one thing. That number, just the Crow Walker did. That's why I tell a lot. I don't play with Billy Dee Dee Band. Because no one don't sing it. People, you want you to hear them. You want you to hear the voice. Yeah. You want you to hear the voice. I don't want to hear the voice. I don't want to hear the voice.
I don't want to hear the voice.
I don't want to hear the voice. You understand?
That's the important part of it.
That's the main thing. They want you to hear the voice of the thing.

You understand? Dave, Dave written a team for Billy. You don't know that. Oh, she ain't going to hear the voice. Dave written a team for you. Give her the voice. Kimmel sang it. You came with Kimmel sang it. But he made the voice for it. Yeah. People want you to hear the voice. Good boy. The people sing it. They know the number, but they want you to sing it the number. Her and her husband do the singing. But that's that main department. So I don't get in that.

I get something. Make me Willie play his solo. I play mine. Then he gets a bit. People want you to sing that thing. Tell them the words what you're doing. If you're saying the right words, what's in that book?
What about fish fries? What were they like? Oh, I don't know.
They never meant that fish fry. Yeah. See, Dick don't think. Dick always go on something different. Well, they want to know all that.

Yeah, Dick. You want me to explain that, Bush? Yeah, I'll tell you. Well, fish fry was nothing but, you know New Orleans, all right. Dick, you're a long way. You know where Jim live at. St. Philip Street, you know where I live at. I'm going to give a fish fry on a Saturday night. You see what you do? You get a wagon lantern light, you know. Put it on your gate with a stick, hold it out like that. And just buy fish, and you tell the people in the neighborhood, that's very few people got our tickets, like when you're going to give a ball, you know. Then you fry, you put the light, and you're going to have a fish fry there tonight. Oh, par. Now the people come there, you get the old river catfish or lake cat, and you get potato salad. And I forgot there's so much a plate it was sold. People that come there and buy the fish, eat it there something. I'm smelling the fish now. Yeah, that's all they meant about fish fry. Anyhow, you could give it in. If it rained, you're flying right in your kitchen. I got you left, buddy. Anyhow, you didn't even have a hall. You didn't have a hall. The law gave you a permit. You're going to get a city hall, I think it was 50 cents or something like that. Well, I'm going to get that permit. Get that permit yourself. Sure, it's all you want.
As you were talking about just close to Walk with Dee, that number would never play out. I don't believe it would, because a lot of people likes it.

See, that's how you tell you, we go out there and play that number. But people, they want to hear someone sing it. But I can't sing it, because I ain't got no voice, and I don't talk too plain. And I ain't got to mess myself up with, but I can play my trombone.

Since you mentioned close to Walk with Dee, you know who I love to play close to Walk with Dee with? This man there. Poes is going to play. This man put close to Walk with Dee with? Just a minute. Let him talk to him. Yeah, I'm going to answer him. No, actually, listen. No, I'm waiting. Poes is going to tell you something about what happened. It was no sound of song. Yeah, well, he's right. Poes is going to know this man to play. That's, that's any time. He's going to know this one.

Just a minute. What I'm going to say is this. This man, put close to Walk with Dee with. I'm going to tell you who I love to play close to Walk with Dee with. This man there. Poes is going to play. segments.title: Punch Miller vs Kid Rena band contest on a Sunday
segments.summary: Jim recalls a street-corner contest between Punch's band and Kid Rena's, with Honky Tonk Town and blues, where cornetists were featured.

segments.title: Boys chased out of the District by police
segments.summary: Young men were run out of the Storyville district with a strap; Percy recalls being too busy with music for girls.

segments.title: Economy Hall balls and French Creole societies
segments.summary: Jim remembers watching the band at Economy Hall balls and why it was named so; many benevolent organizations kept the bands busy.

segments.title: Benevolent societies, dues and funeral brass bands
segments.summary: The men explain how societies paid for funerals and brass bands through monthly dues.

segments.title: King Oliver and learning by stealing
segments.summary: Brief talk of King Oliver, and Jim says he learned by listening and stealing from other players.

segments.title: New Orleans as one big jazz band: house parties, lawn parties, Milneburg camps
segments.summary: With no radio or TV, house and lawn parties and lake camps at Milneburg, West End and Bucktown kept bands playing.

segments.title: Long hours and relaxed playing then versus loud music now
segments.summary: A speaker contrasts today's constant tourist playing with the old long nights, few tunes an hour and strolling from camp to camp.

segments.title: Labor Day parades and all-night fairground dances
segments.summary: Societies' bands met at Elk's Place, paraded all day, then played at the fairground until morning.

segments.title: Melody in Dixieland brass music versus rock and roll
segments.summary: The men prefer playing a melody people can follow; one keeps a rock instrument only just in case.

segments.title: Playing Germany and Europe in 1966-67: music as a universal language
segments.summary: Jim tells of tours with the All-Star Band in 1966 and George Lewis in 1967, and audiences who understood the music without the language.

segments.title: Sam Morgan's band, Creole society dances and waltzes
segments.summary: Jim describes dance bands of the 1920s, Sam Morgan and Kid Rena as draws, the social club halls and shouters and waltzes.

segments.title: Circus music and young audiences on Preservation Hall tours
segments.summary: Jim explains what 'circus music' meant and tells young listeners the music was danced to at slow tempos.

segments.title: Rock and roll musicians met in San Francisco
segments.summary: Percy defends his own way of playing and recalls meeting rock players in San Francisco with large equipment.

segments.title: Whether early jazz grew from brass band and march music
segments.summary: The interviewer asks how much jazz came from brass band music; a speaker explains the doubled march rhythm and improvisation.

segments.title: Hymn books, spirituals and the Singing River legend
segments.summary: The men discuss jazz coming from church hymns and slavery-era singing, and Jim tells of the Singing River in Mississippi.

segments.title: Audiences want a vocal on the number
segments.summary: Percy and Jim say people want to hear the voice sing the words, and describe sharing solos in the band.

segments.chapter: Social life of old New Orleans
segments.title: What a New Orleans fish fry was
segments.summary: Jim explains how a neighborhood fish fry was held: a lantern on the gate, fried catfish, potato salad and a city permit.

segments.title: Just a Closer Walk With Thee and playing it with Percy
segments.summary: The men talk about the hymn that draws requests for singing, and Jim praises Percy's key and harmony on it.

segments.title: Disneyland finale with Louis Armstrong and the key of D flat
segments.summary: Percy and Jim recall the Disneyland river parade with five bands and five trumpets, and a difficult key.

segments.title: Four-piece band at Brennan's and on WDSU television
segments.summary: The men recall a four-piece Saturday television show and playing at Brennan's, with Jim's illness on a job.

segments.chapter: Social life of old New Orleans
segments.title: Piano and guitar players at fish fries
segments.summary: Fish fries seldom hired bands; a piano or a passing guitarist would play.

segments.chapter: Social life of old New Orleans
segments.title: Safety, summer nights and entertainment in old New Orleans
segments.summary: Jim and others recall doors left open, cabarets and dance halls everywhere, and worry about youngsters today.

segments.chapter: Social life of old New Orleans
segments.title: Honky tonks and cabarets
segments.summary: Percy and Jim describe the honky tonks as cabarets with dancing and girls.

segments.chapter: Social life of old New Orleans
segments.title: Storyville district: barrel houses, boundaries and respect
segments.summary: Jim says the district ran him out as a boy, names its boundaries, and the men recall its people as decent.

segments.chapter: Social life of old New Orleans
segments.title: Women in ballrooms and barrooms
segments.summary: Speakers say trouble began once ladies were admitted to the ballroom and barroom.

segments.title: Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith and women who ran their own groups
segments.summary: Asked about women blues singers, the men say they never worked with them; the singers had their own groups.

segments.title: Earl Humphrey on the road, recordings and the Solace Green band
segments.summary: The men discuss Percy's brother Earl, a drummer who toured and recorded with women singers, and a 1932 sighting of him.

segments.title: What Chris Kelly wore on jobs
segments.summary: Jim and Percy say Chris Kelly wore ordinary black clothes and bad shoes, and was a blues man.

segments.title: Uniforms of the Piron and Tuxedo bands
segments.summary: Cie Frazier describes Piron's checkered coats at Suburban Gardens in 1928 and subbing with the Original Tuxedo band.

segments.title: Giving dancers slow numbers: feeling the audience
segments.summary: Percy and Jim say audiences want to be played slow numbers, and a musician must feel the crowd.

segments.title: Why pianists were called Professor
segments.summary: A question on the term Professor is answered: pianists in Storyville sporting houses were so named; the rest is murmur.

segments.chapter: Army service in World War I
segments.title: Learning trombone in the army band in France
segments.summary: Jim tells how an officer, Lieutenant Lion, took him on and taught him trombone, and the band played around France.

segments.chapter: Army service in World War I
segments.title: Landing at Newport News and the camp commander story
segments.summary: Jim recalls landing at Newport News and a colored camp commander being made to dig trenches.

segments.title: Playing quadrilles
segments.summary: The men say they have played quadrilles, which they call a beautiful dance.

segments.title: Would they choose music again
segments.summary: The men say they have no regrets and would play until they cannot.

segments.title: Banjo and tenor guitar talk, and close
segments.summary: Logistics, seating and mic placement, a 1918 banjo, remarks on tenor guitar and a final tune.
